fullText:
Anthropic ​argued designation as ‘supply-chain risk’ could cost billions ‌in lost business ‌and reputational harm

A US judge ruled on Thursday that the Trump administration broke the law when it designated Anthropic as a supply chain risk earlier this year, finding that the government had unlawfully targeted the AI firm for refusing to comply with defense department demands.

“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Judge Rita Lin said in a 59-page decision.

Lin’s ruling barred the federal agencies named in the lawsuit from enforcing Donald Trump’s order to stop using Anthropic’s tools and overturned the designation of the company as a “supply chain risk” by the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. The status, usually reserved for foreign firms, would have blocked government agencies from doing business with Anthropic.

The case emerged out of a months-long feud between Anthropic and the Pentagon at the start of the year. Anthropic refused to allow the government to use its Claude AI model for fully autonomous lethal weapons or domestic mass surveillance, resulting in Hegseth accusing the company of “arrogance and betrayal”.

Lin put a temporary pause on the government’s punitive measures in March, stating that the government’s actions looked like an attempt to “cripple Anthropic” for exercising its first amendment rights. The ruling this week makes that temporary suspension permanent, although the government may appeal.

“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said.

Lin’s ruling is a victory for Anthropic, which had warned that the supply chain risk designation could cost the company billions of dollars and complicate its business model. Anthropic is also planning an IPO later this year that could value the firm at $2tn and raise $100bn, exceeding the record set by SpaceX in June.

Anthropic still faces legal hurdles related to the supply chain risk designation, however, as the outcome of a second lawsuit in Washington DC is still pending. That case will be heard by a three-judge panel, two of whom are Trump appointees who have expressed skepticism about Anthropic’s arguments.

Anthropic says that AI models are not reliable enough to be safely used in autonomous weapons ‌and that it opposes domestic surveillance as a violation of rights, but the Pentagon says private companies should not be able to constrain military action.

In its 9 March lawsuit, Anthropic alleged the government violated its right to free speech under the first amendment of the constitution by retaliating against its views on AI safety. The company said it was not given a chance to dispute the designation, in violation of its fifth amendment right to due process.

“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice,” Lin said, “the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless.”

Anthropic’s designation was the first time a US company had been publicly categorized as a supply-chain risk under an obscure government-procurement statute aimed at protecting military systems ​from foreign sabotage.

With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Trump’s Cabinet is fanning out to help juice the base. It’s not going as planned.
description: Trump is deploying Cabinet members across the country to sell his record ahead of the midterms. In some cases, they’re ending up on the back foot.
fullText:
President Donald Trump is fanning out his Cabinet across the country to sell his accomplishments and shore up key constituencies ahead of the midterms.

It isn't quite working out that way.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited New Hampshire last week to tout natural gas pipelines and got hit with questions about $4 gasoline prices. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins was in Iowa over the weekend ostensibly to rally farmers and instead had to defend Trump's decision to import foreign beef, which sparked outcry among cattle ranchers.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., in Florida to talk about school nutrition, faced questions about a Pennsylvania measles outbreak and ended up in a protracted fight with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro over whether the virus is responsible for two deaths.

Even Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a veteran of Wall Street, is struggling to win over some of his former colleagues, who are skeptical of his "economic D-Day" plan to end the Iran war and downright hostile to his attempt to lower the interest rate the federal government pays on long-term debt.

The Cabinet kerfuffle comes at a time when the president's envoys are needed most. The midterms are less than three months away, the president's approval rating is near record-lows and the White House is on a mission to remind voters of all it believes it has accomplished in the last two years, including a spate of tax cuts, improved border security and reductions in violent crime.

The Cabinet barnstorming is key to the administration's midterms messaging strategy. Secretaries have used visits to promote administration policy and gin up local news coverage.

But Rollins' recent visit to Iowa is emblematic of the broad discontent the administration is contending with, and the ways its surrogates are being knocked off message by an electorate that is deeply skeptical of some of its policies. That includes some historically loyal constituencies: Ranchers and farmers are furious over Trump's recent decision to import 300,000 metric tons of beef and sell them at discounted prices. Rollins did not disown the decision — defending Trump's focus on lowering prices for consumers — but didn't exactly embrace it either, telling reporters earlier this week that she hadn't discussed the specific policy with the president.

"If you just look at how it's animating people here, if you just look at the breadth of the headlines coming out from it, it's a challenge. It has legs, to be honest," said one Republican operative in Iowa, granted anonymity to address the fallout from the beef announcement. "You don't have to go further than to look at how [Democratic gubernatorial candidate] Rob Sand and them are using it. They clearly think it's an issue."

Had Trump not made the announcement, which is intended to lower grocery prices, "it might have been just more of a routine thing like, 'Heck yeah we want her here,'" the person added.

After publication, a Department of Agriculture spokesperson, granted anonymity to discuss Rollins' views of her engagement with farmers, said in a statement that Rollins "has treasured the thousands of conversations, has taken copious notes, and even follows up with every farmer in each of her roundtables after the trips."

"The conversations are always productive and respectful as we work to bring farmers and ranchers back to the center of federal policy making," the spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin is making it harder for communities to oppose new data centers at the very moment there is a bipartisan outcry against them. And immigration hardliners have soured on Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, as MAGA continues to rail against what they view as lagging deportation numbers. The administration this week launched a messaging blitz to tout record ICE arrests and efforts to clamp down on legal immigration — in what appears to be a bid to rebut the criticism.

"Everyone in MAGA knows Markwayne Mullin is a squish on immigration enforcement — look at the lack of [temporary protected status] removals or work site raids — they have to hide him," said Steve Bannon, former White House chief strategist. "Bobby, Bessent, Marco you can promote, DHS no way."

Chandler Rebel, spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, said in a statement that under Mullin, "ICE is working around the clock every day to arrest and deport the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from American communities. The results speak for themselves."

"We are all focused on delivering on the President's mission to deport illegal aliens and protect the homeland. Anyone who says otherwise is just trying to sow division and create an illusion of chaos," Rebel said.

Still, the litany of frustrations and distractions underscore the challenge facing the Trump administration as it works to stay on message in the final sprint ahead of the midterms.

"Instead of assuring voters, they end up raising more questions and sometimes showing the liability that this entire administration has across the board. It's hard to point to a good spokesman or even a high point in this administration right now, and certainly the polls reflect it," said Matthew Bartlett, a Republican strategist who served in Trump's first administration. "So I'm just not sure that sending every Cabinet member and their mother out on the campaign trail is going to help. Instead of solving a problem, you end up creating divisions."

White House aides pushed back on the idea that Cabinet secretaries haven't been on message, arguing that they frequently discuss many topics of importance to the American people.

"President Trump has assembled the most talented Cabinet in American history who work every day to implement his common sense, America First agenda," said White House spokesperson Olivia Wales.

And Cabinet members do have their strengths and can still call attention to administration achievements.

On Wednesday, Kennedy was in Tampa with Florida Sen. Ashley Moody to unveil a new school nutrition program. The secretary has often been deployed to persuade MAHA voters that Trump is in their corner even as some are disappointed with the administration on certain issues, such as its protection of glyphosate.

One person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that Kennedy in particular remains a key asset to the administration because he is the rare Cabinet member with his own distinct constituency, and dismissed concerns that the measles outbreak would overshadow the secretary's efforts to communicate the administration's message.

"Bobby's super popular with huge-ass swaths of the party," the person said. "Sometimes you have to be a little more strategic, but he is very well liked."

HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard, in a statement, noted that Kennedy in August completed an 18-day tour "to bring the MAHA agenda directly to communities" and said that he would "continue engaging directly with Americans while delivering on President Trump's promise to Make America Healthy Again."

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth received high marks when he rallied at a veteran-focused fund-raising event at the Iowa State Fair alongside Reps. Zach Nunn, who is running for governor, Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a vulnerable Republican up for re-election, and Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for a competitive, open Senate seat.

And the Cabinet appears poised to keep traveling. Bessent is headed to North Carolina to address the Charlotte Economics Club as many Republicans continue to see the Treasury secretary as a strong messenger on economic issues — as well as girding against criticism of the Iran war.

"Bessent is such a good Swiss Army knife on issues and as a communicator because he projects confidence and competence at the same time on such a range of topics," said Matt Whitlock, a GOP strategist and former National Republican Senatorial Committee senior adviser. "Whether it's broad questions about the economy or how we are actively putting pressure on Iran, he always seems to have a pretty good answer and idea for what the administration is doing."

A Treasury official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that Bessent, as he travels the country, is "seeing something national reporters continue to miss: real people aren't living online or caught up in the D.C. bubble. They're focused on their families, their jobs, and the opportunities that President Trump's policies are creating."

Iowa Republicans may be less thrilled about Rollins, who is set to return to the state on Tuesday to speak at the Farm Progress Show.

"Trump has a good story to tell on the economy with respect to the tax cut and with respect to the investment that's coming," said economist Stephen Moore, a former Trump adviser. But "if people are going to start confronting her on beef prices or egg prices or whatever it might be, it's better to avoid being in the spotlight so you don't get set up."

title: White House silent on Iran-Oman Hormuz plan Tehran says would ban US warships
description: Iran says a proposed Strait of Hormuz framework with Oman would exclude military vessels, but the White House won't say if Trump would accept it.
fullText:
The Trump administration spent months insisting Iran did not control passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

But after Iran and Oman unveiled a proposed framework that Tehran says would exclude military vessels if finalized, the White House would not say whether President Donald Trump would accept any restriction on U.S. warships under the arrangement.

U.S. Central Command, meanwhile, rejected Iran's underlying claim of authority.

"Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz," CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told Fox News Digital. "The strait is an international waterway that commercial vessels continue to transit with U.S. military assistance."

Iran Fails To Strike Deal With Us As Deadline Passes And Trump Calls For 'White Flag Of Surrender'

Fox News Digital asked whether Trump would accept a restriction on U.S. military vessels if the proposal becomes binding, whether American forces would be expected to comply and whether U.S. warships retain the right to operate in the strait regardless of any future arrangement. The White House did not respond.

Hawkins said U.S. forces have helped nearly 1,500 vessels transit the strait since early May.

The silence marks a shift after months in which the administration publicly challenged Iranian efforts to dictate passage through Hormuz. Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeatedly called a proposed toll system illegal and unacceptable, while Trump threatened Oman this month if it "gets in the way" of a U.S. deal with Iran.

Trump Threatens 'Unprecedented' Economic Consequences For Any Nation Aiding Iran

The administration has also spent months applying military and economic pressure aimed at reopening the strait on U.S. terms. American forces have struck Iranian military targets, protected commercial shipping and maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, while the administration expanded sanctions through its new Operation Economic Outcast campaign.

Those measures have helped push some ships back through Hormuz, but traffic remains far below pre-war levels.

Oil flows through the strait stood Monday at about 5 million barrels per day, down from more than 20 million barrels per day before the war, according to Reuters, which cited provisional Vortexa tracking data.

Iran is now pursuing a reopening arrangement that, by its account, would preserve a measure of control over the waterway while excluding foreign military vessels.

Oman and Iran announced a proposed framework Monday to reopen the strait through a joint temporary navigational corridor and a joint mine-clearing project.

Their joint statement said technical talks would continue on a permanent corridor, future administration of the strait, traffic management and security services, leaving key terms unresolved.

Iranian officials filled in some of those blanks Tuesday.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the temporary arrangement would route commercial ships entering the Persian Gulf through Iranian waters, with outbound traffic moving through Iranian and Omani waters. He said the proposal would exclude military vessels if it becomes binding.

Separately, Sepah News, an outlet run by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, quoted IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi as saying Iran and Oman had reached agreements on "each country's share of the strait's waters" and the two countries' "share of its revenues."

Mohebbi also accused the U.S. of obstructing the talks.

Us Claws Back Key Concession To Iran After Fresh Attacks On Commercial Ships In Strait Of Hormuz

But Oman's public statement did not mention a military-vessel ban, transit fees or revenue sharing, and described the framework as proposed. Iranian officials also told Reuters the arrangement was not yet final.

That leaves the arrangement's most consequential question unresolved: whether Iran can use the emerging commercial shipping framework to restrict American military access to the strait — and what the Trump administration intends to do if Tehran tries.

title: President Donald Trump loses again in bid to erase his hush money conviction
description: A federal judge on Friday once again spurned Donald Trump’s effort to erase his hush money conviction, rejecting the president’s bid to move the state court case to federal court and have it dismissed...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — A federal judge on Friday once again spurned Donald Trump's effort to erase his hush money conviction, rejecting the president's bid to move the state court case to federal court and have it dismissed on presidential immunity grounds.

Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein reiterated his earlier finding against Trump, saying that the reasons Trump cited for renewing his request were "neither new nor legally sufficient."

The judge added: "He has failed to show good cause and diligence."

It is the third time Hellerstein has blocked Trump from having the U.S. District Court in Manhattan seize control of the case from the New York court where he was tried and convicted.

And, like before, Trump will appeal, according to a spokesperson for his legal team who called Hellerstein's ruling "baseless and lawless."

"The Supreme Court's historic decision on Immunity, the Federal and New York State Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed," a statement issued on behalf of the legal team said. "President Trump will be filing a powerful appeal, and will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn."

The guilty verdict, reached in May 2024 while Trump was between terms, made him the first former — and now current — U.S. president to be convicted of a crime. Trump is also challenging his conviction through the state court appellate process, which is pending.

Hellerstein's decision came after a federal appeals court last year ordered him to reconsider his prior denial. The judge previewed his ruling during oral arguments in February, slamming Trump's lawyers for legal maneuvers that amounted to taking "two bites at the apple."

State prosecutors did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump was convicted in May 2024 of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to conceal a $130,000 hush money payment to adult film actor Stormy Daniels, whose claim of a sexual encounter with Trump a decade earlier had threatened to upend his 2016 presidential campaign.

Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge, which left his conviction intact but spared him any punishment. He had long denied Daniels' claim and said he did nothing wrong. He has sought to get the conviction overturned both by attempting to move the case to federal court and through the appeals process in state court, which is pending.

Hellerstein rejected Trump's requests to move the case twice before. The first was after Trump's March 2023 indictment. The second was after Trump's trial, as his lawyers sought to nix his conviction in the wake of the Supreme Court's July 2024 ruling that presidents and ex-presidents can't be prosecuted for official acts and prosecutors can't use official acts as evidence that unofficial actions were illegal.

Trump appealed Hellerstein's post-trial ruling and, last November, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ordered the judge to reconsider his decision, finding that he had failed to consider "important issues relevant" to the president's request to move the case.

A three-judge appellate panel said it expressed no view on how he should rule but instructed Hellerstein to closely review evidence that Trump claimed was related to official acts and whether Trump could argue those actions were taken as part of his White House duties.

The judges also instructed Hellerstein to determine if Trump had "diligently sought" to have the case moved to federal court and whether the case can even be moved to federal court now that Trump has been convicted and sentenced in state court.

During oral arguments in February, Hellerstein took issue with the Trump legal team's decision-making after the Supreme Court ruling.

Instead of immediately seeking to move the case to federal court, he noted, Trump's lawyers first asked the trial judge in state court, Juan Merchan, to throw out the verdict on immunity grounds. Normally, such a request must be made within 30 days of an arraignment, but a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C. has ruled that exceptions can be made if "good cause" is shown.

Trump, a Republican, did not attend the arguments.

Trump lawyer Jeffrey Wall argued that prosecutors rushed to trial instead of waiting for the Supreme Court's presidential immunity decision and that Trump's legal team was crunched for time after the high court's ruling because his sentencing was scheduled for just 10 days later.

Trump's lawyers did not ask Hellerstein to intervene until nearly two months later, while their request to Merchan was still pending. The judge called that a "strategic decision" and suggested that by going to the state court first, Trump's lawyers cost him the right to pursue remedies in federal court.

"No, your honor," Wall replied. "It is what any sensible litigant would do" in that situation.

"That is a decision on your part," the judge added. "You didn't have to do that. You could have come right to the federal court. Just by filing a notice of removal, there would be no sentencing."

Trump's lawyers "made a choice," Hellerstein said, "and you sought two bites at the apple."

In his written ruling Friday, Hellerstein said Trump was asking for a "'second bite at the apple,' a result the law disfavors."

The judge added that "Trump's delay in filing for removal constitutes a 'quintessential strategic decision,' and the 'fact that he later came to view that decision as a poor one is not sufficient, by itself, to establish cause.'"

title: Trump administration seeks to restrict internships for international students
description: (This Aug 27 story has been republished, with no changes to text.)
fullText:
(This Aug 27 story has been republished, with no changes to text.)

WASHINGTON, Aug 27 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration has issued a memo for universities that seeks to restrict issuance of certain internship work ‌authorizations for international students as the federal government warned that colleges not complying with the regulations may lose certification ‌to enroll foreign students.

The federal memo dated August 24 said the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, which is part of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement ​agency, has "observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorizations that appear to violate regulatory requirements which permit CPT only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum."

"Failure to comply with SEVP regulations may result in an institution losing certification to enroll foreign students," the memo said.

It resulted in some schools, including the University of California, Los Angeles and the University of California, Berkeley, pausing certain ‌applications for work authorizations for international students.

"UCLA ⁠has paused certain Curricular Practical Training authorizations while it reviews recent federal guidance and determines next steps," a UCLA spokesperson said.

UC Berkeley's international office said the August 24 memo was "more narrow in focus, more ⁠direct, and includes content that is more restrictive in nature." The federal government had also issued an earlier memo in mid-August.

UC Berkeley's international office said it is unlikely that it will process certain work authorization applications "in the near future" and urged those international students to plan ​accordingly.

It said ​it will continue processing "degree-requirement" CPT as normal and would resume processing "Doctoral ​Dissertation and Master's Thesis Research CPT." The office said ‌it would consult legal experts to develop new processes aligning with new federal requirements.

"Nothing about these regulations has changed," the Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent, said in a statement. "However, schools and employers should consider themselves on notice: under President Trump, abuse of this generous system will no longer be tolerated."

Trump has targeted universities with probes and funding threats over issues like pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel's assault on Gaza, diversity initiatives, climate programs and transgender policies. Rights advocates have raised free speech, academic freedom ‌and due process concerns.

Separately, the U.S. Justice Department alleged on Thursday admissions ​practices at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Services favored ​Black and Hispanic applicants, citing findings of a probe ​as the Trump administration continued its diversity crackdown.

"We are disappointed by the DOJ's conclusions, which we believe ‌are incorrect," the university said, saying the admissions policies ​were in compliance with law and ​not discriminatory.

The Justice Department has alleged similar bias at other schools, saying the department aims for settlement talks. If those efforts fail, the department will file suit, it said.

Trump's administration has also revoked visas of student protesters over pro-Palestinian ​protests that it casts as antisemitic and ‌sympathetic to extremists.

Protesters, including some Jewish groups, say opposition to Israel's assault on Gaza and its occupation of ​Palestinian territories is not antisemitic and advocacy for Palestinian rights is not the same as supporting extremism.

title: Democratic strategist: ‘Something’s going on’ when Trump ‘can only deliver 52 percent’ in South Carolina
description: Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha said Wednesday he expected President Trump’s endorsement of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to lead to a wider margin of victory for her in Tuesday’s GOP Senate runoff. ...
fullText:
Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha said Wednesday he expected President Trump's endorsement of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to lead to a wider margin of victory for her in Tuesday's GOP Senate runoff.

Rocha explained in an appearance on NewsNation's "Cuomo" that he thought Graham would win but "didn't think it would be this close" given Trump backed the senator.

She defeated Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) by just less than 5 points in the state's runoff, securing a spot on the general election ballot in place of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The GOP nominee will now face Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election, with Decision Desk HQ giving the Republican an 81 percent chance to win as of Tuesday.

Rocha, who advised Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) during his two unsuccessful presidential campaigns, noted that Darline Graham's narrow runoff victory does not lead him to believe Andrews will win.

"But I am going to say something's going on when Donald Trump can only deliver 52 percent," he told host Chris Cuomo, while qualifying, "I get it was a special election. She's only been running a little bit."

The strategist also noted more than 40 percent of voters in June's GOP primary voted for a candidate other than Lindsey Graham, an election held just more than a month before the four-term senator died of an aortic dissection.

"But Donald Trump should be getting 70, 80, 90 percent in a Republican primary," Rocha argued.

The president hit the trail last week to stump for Darline Graham, venturing to the coastal town of Myrtle Beach, S.C. During a rally alongside the newest senator, he urged Republicans to turn out in the midterms.

"What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," Trump said at the time.

Graham won Horry County, where Myrtle Beach is located, by more than 46 points over Norman. The senator was also victorious in 34 of 46 counties in the Palmetto State, according to data from the South Carolina Election Commission.

The victory was seen as a significant flex by Trump after Graham made a major gaffe a week earlier on the debate state while dodging a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

More than 369,000 Republicans in the state cast a ballot in the runoff, accounting for roughly 12 percent of the more than 3 million total registered voters in the state, per the state election commission.

Democrats have suggested Graham's win could give their party a chance at taking the seat, though that appears unlikely.

Conservative talk show host Mark Davis, who also appeared as a guest on Cuomo's show, defended the GOP hopeful as being the "deep underdog" in the race "because nobody knew who she was on July 10, the day before Lindsey died."

"For Trump to endorse her and bring her across the finish line is a major, major bit of evidence to the strength of his endorsement," he added.

title: Republican governor asks his AG to look into ‘aggressive’ behavior by Trump admin’s election monitors
description: Wyoming’s Republican Gov. Mark Gordon voiced concerns about the Justice Department election monitors who observed the primary election in his state last week, saying he’s asked his attorney general to...
fullText:
Wyoming's Republican Gov. Mark Gordon voiced concerns about the Justice Department election monitors who observed the primary election in his state last week, saying he's asked his attorney general to look into their "aggressive" behavior.

The Justice Department sent two Civil Rights Division attorneys to Laramie County, Wyoming, which includes the state capital of Cheyenne. But some officials, including the state attorney general, weren't made aware of the move in advance, Gordon said at a state canvassing board meeting Wednesday.

"It sounded like the behavior of the observers was a bit aggressive," Gordon said, adding, "It just was irregular and, and I have asked the attorney general to start looking into … the nature of the visits and all that sort of stuff."

The DOJ, when reached for comment, pointed CNN to an August 18 statement from Wyoming US Attorney Darin Smith: "Voters deserve absolute confidence that their ballots are secure and their voices are heard without interference…. We are working alongside local officials to ensure every lawful vote is protected."

CNN has reached out to the governor's office for comment.

The DOJ said it has sent more than 80 monitors to seven states so far this year for primary elections, as of Tuesday. The department has said it would send about 1,000 monitors to polling sites in November.

Gordon's criticism comes as President Donald Trump continues to sow doubt about elections. Earlier this year, he baselessly alleged there was cheating in the Los Angeles mayoral primary election before the DOJ sent a prosecutor to observe ballot processing. The president also still claims, without evidence, that the 2020 election he lost to former President Joe Biden was rigged.

Democrats and voting rights activists raised concerns last year, ahead of the off-year elections, that the monitors could be used to undermine the voting process or as a precursor to sow doubts about the election. But the Trump administration had insisted monitors are being sent out in line with decadeslong federal monitoring practices.

Gordon said he isn't against the idea of election monitors, but raised concerns that the "behavior" of the ones deployed to Wyoming "seemed to exceed what the authority that Congress had given them was."

"I'm not saying anything went wrong or anything else, and I certainly think that the conduct of this election was phenomenal," Gordon said. But, he added, "I don't like the federal government coming in and taking our votes."

CNN's Hannah Rabinowitz and Fredreka Schouten contributed to this report.

title: Trump Is Waging War on Haitians
description: Sasha...
fullText:
In Springfield, Ohio, ICE agents are targeting a community that Trump has been villainizing since 2024.

Late last week, volunteers working with the Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio, were inundated with calls about men being arrested and separated from their families. One of those detained was a pastor, Gilbert Joubert Adrien. Joubert Adrien, who is the minister of a church of 130 people, was, apparently, snatched by ICE agents while at a gas station. He is just one of several dozen Haitians to be targeted by ICE in Springfield in the past week, according to monitoring groups such as G92 and the Haitian Bridge Alliance.

Haitians in Springfield have been the center of some of the cruelest xenophobic behaviors of the Trump era. Perhaps you will remember the 2024 presidential campaign, during which JD Vance and Donald Trump made up false rumors about Haitians in the city “eating dogs and cats.” Trump doubled down on this outlandish claim during his televised debate with Kamala Harris; Vance admitted that the allegations were likely false but nevertheless went out of his way to justify his circulation of these slanderous allegations.

Now the administration is unleashing the full force of ICE on this same community, launching what can only be described as an officially sanctioned pogrom against people whose offense seems mainly to be that they are members of a race and a nation that Trump regards with peculiar contempt and animus. “These are people who fled for their lives,” Guerline Jozef, of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told me. “Some of them still have pending asylum claims, which means the government is violating due process.”

Similar attacks against Haitians are occurring around the country. In San Diego, advocates for the Haitian community have been using social media to report dozens of ICE kidnappings over the past two weeks along El Cajon Boulevard, and in the City Heights and Lemon Grove neighborhoods. In Flatbush, Brooklyn, the epicenter of the Big Apple’s Haitian community, businesses report that fewer customers are coming in, with community members afraid to be seen in public lest ICE snatch them. In the days after the Supreme Court ruling, the New York City Public Advocate’s office reported increased ICE activity in the neighborhood. In southern Florida, the Haitian Bridge Alliance reports that a surge of immigrants Haitians have been arrested and placed into deportation proceedings since the Supreme Court ruling. Jozef tells me of Haitian meatpackers and poultry workers in Salisbury, Maryland, and Virginia, who have also been snatched by ICE. She marvels, she says at “the cruelty, the inhumanity, the terror in what they are inflicting on the community.” And, she says, the Alliance expects things to only get worse, “even more casualties, more cruelties, more children being left without their parents.”

During Trump 1.0, the MAGA leader listed Haiti among the “shithole” countries of the world whose people he didn’t want immigrating to the US. One of the immediate consequences of Trump’s loathing of Haitians was a shutting of the southern border to Haitian men traveling north after they had been booted out of Brazil during a particular moment of economic crisis. In 2018, I interviewed many Haitian women in San Diego who had been stranded in the city with their young children, while their husbands, boyfriends, and teenage sons were either detained in US detention centers after asking for asylum or were stuck in limbo in Tijuana and unable to reunite with their female relatives in the United States.

Fast-forward eight years and that animus is, at speed, upending hundreds of thousands of lives and causing untold economic chaos in communities around the United States. It goes without saying that the vast majority of the more than 300,000 Haitians Trump is targeting around the country are law-abiding members of society. Until the US Supreme Court’s hard-right majority allowed the administration to shred Haitians’ Temporary Protected Status, they were living and working in the country entirely legally, working in industries such as home healthcare and construction, in restaurants and warehouses. They had the required work permits and they had Social Security numbers. Now their papers have been deemed void, in a way not dissimilar to how German Jews were deprived of citizenship rights in the early years of Nazi rule; their status has been revoked, and they are being quite literally hunted by ICE, fitted with ankle monitors, or simply thrown into harsh detention centers. Many of them are being summarily flown back to Haiti—a country with a supposedly transitional government presided over by an unelected council, which has no democratic mandate and that exists largely in name only, its writ hardly present in many parts of the nation; afflicted with desperate poverty; and experiencing daily terror inflicted by some of the most violent gangs on earth—and left to fend for themselves however they can.

In a single day’s haul last week, ICE deported more than 160 people back to Haiti, according to reporting by the Miami Herald. They were dropped off in Port-au-Prince with nothing but their wits to survive on. Days later, gangs in the nearby city of Kenscoff killed 47 people and kidnapped many others—further evidence, if any were needed, of just how dangerous conditions are in the country that these deportees are now being sent to. Instead of pulling back, the administration doubled down. On Thursday, the The New York Times reported that team Trump was planning weekly deportation flights to Haiti.The real risk of violent death faced by these deportees is, clearly, of absolutely no concern to the masters of Trump’s deportation machine.

It is hard to overemphasize just how authoritarian and cruel this all is. In its vast scale, we can liken it to Stalin’s projects of uprooting hundreds of thousands and millions at a go, and ordering them to relocate without consideration for impact on families or on community. It is, too, redolent of some early Nazi practices: In the deliberate humiliation ritual of fitting law-abiding people, recently deemed enemies of the state, with ankle monitors—all-too-visible markers of “otherness”—simply because of who they are, it is redolent of the Nazi’s decision, early in Hitler’s reign, to force Jews to wear the identifying tag of the yellow Star of David sewn onto their clothing.

Good Germans, back then, either turned a blind eye to what was happening, cheered it on, or, if they were government officials, rationalized the implementation of these vile mandates by avowing that they were only obeying orders. Today, I fear, Good Americans are doing much the same thing: Some simply prefer not to see; others—the MAGA diehards—cheer on this sadism; and still others, including those working for government agencies that are increasingly made dirty by Trump’s fanaticism, rationalize the unjustifiable by saying that this is all above their pay grade and that they are simply doing what they have been ordered to do.

There is, in the United States these days, more than a whiff of Hannah Arendt’s banality of evil. Entirely atrocious things—things that will haunt subsequent generations—are being done in our names; yet the temptation is that we get on with our daily lives and ignore the screams of terror and of despair from the victims of Trump’s unleashed gestapo.

title: Al Michaels cracks Lake Ontario joke amid ongoing name controversy
description: Lake Ontario, which President Trump wants to rename Lake America amid an ongoing clash with Canada, was the subject of a joke from the broadcaster.

It only took one possession for veteran play-by-play man Al Michaels to get into midseason form during Amazon Prime Video's preseason "Thursday Night Football" broadcast.

The broadcast was coming back from a commercial after the Browns opened the game with a touchdown from Dillon Gabriel to Luke Floriea. It showed an aerial shot of Huntington Bank Field, which abuts Lake Erie.
